title: Nahum
subtitle: the fall of the city of blood
lead: Nahum is a short book with one subject: the end of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. For about a century Assyria had ruled the Near East, and Judah had paid it tribute and borne its yoke. Nahum is a poem of the coming end. It begins with a hymn to the LORD, a jealous God who takes vengeance, comes in storm and flood, and is also a stronghold for those who shelter in him. It goes on to pictures of the attack on Nineveh (chapter 2) and a funeral song with woes (chapter 3). In the middle a runner crosses the mountains with good news for Judah.

Nahum is the second book of the Twelve that is about Nineveh. Jonah, set a century or more earlier, tells how the city was warned, turned back, and was spared. Nahum says what happened afterward. The two books end the same way, with a question: Jonah with God's question about pity for the city, and Nahum with a question about whether anyone has escaped its wickedness. The book is hard, its images of vengeance and of a shamed woman are among the roughest in the Bible, and this Plain does not soften them. It tries to say who first heard them and why.
facts: Nahum of Elkosh, about whom nothing else is known. The place Elkosh is unknown (Galilee, Judah and northern Iraq have each been proposed). Jewish tradition says the Men of the Great Assembly wrote the Twelve (Bava Batra 15a).

After the fall of Thebes (about 663 BC, 3:8-10) and before or close to the fall of Nineveh (612 BC). The commonest estimates fall in the 650s to 620s BC. Josephus (Antiquities 9.11.3) puts Nahum under Jotham, about 115 years before the fall, which does not fit 3:8-10.
Judah under Assyrian rule (1:12-13), and Nineveh on the Tigris. Thebes in Egypt is the example (3:8-10).
Poetry throughout. A hymn (1:2-8), an oracle, a victory song and a funeral song. The heading calls it an "oracle" (massa') and a "book of the vision."
Hebrew. The poetry is vivid and sound-driven; a few words are found only here (peladot in 2:3, the covering in 2:5, Huzzab in 2:7), and 1:9-14 is hard.
English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1-13 is Hebrew 2:2-14. Hebrew chapter 1 therefore has 14 verses, chapter 2 has 14, and chapter 3 has 19. This site uses the English numbers.

The seventh of the Twelve Minor Prophets in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum...) and the seventh in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Nahum...). In the Greek order Jonah comes right before Nahum.

The Leningrad Codex (the base); Swete's printed Septuagint, mainly Codex Vaticanus; printouts of the Murabba'at scroll Mur88 and the Qumran scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g) from the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (ETCBC dss). The Greek scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) and the Nahum Pesher (4Q169) are not in that printout and are cited only from their editions. The printout shows only Mur88 and 4Q82 for Nahum; whether other Twelve scrolls from Qumran (4QXIIa, c, d) contain Nahum was not checked, and nothing is said of them here.
authorship: Nahum of Elkosh wrote the oracle in the 600s BC. Jewish tradition counts the book as part of the one scroll of the Twelve, which the Men of the Great Assembly wrote down (Bava Batra 15a). Christian commentators from Jerome on have taken the author as the prophet named in the heading. They place Elkosh in Galilee (Jerome, who says a guide showed him the village) or in the tribe of Simeon (the Lives of the Prophets; Calvin wrongly gives Simeon as Jerome's view); the place is unknown (see the note at 1:1).

Most critics accept a prophet of the 600s BC, with later editing. Hermann Gunkel (1893) argued that 1:2-8 is an older partial alphabet poem put at the head of the book. Alfred Haldar (1947) read the book as the liturgy of a cult prophet. Others see it as a single composition. A few read the fall as already past. The Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls give no sign of a different book.

audience.to: Judeans in the 600s BC, living under Assyrian rule or its memory, are the commonest answer. They had paid tribute for a century, seen Samaria fall (722-721 BC) and Jerusalem spared in 701 BC. The heading addresses Nineveh, but the book speaks about the city to a Judean audience, with Judah addressed in 1:12-13 and 15.
audience.why: To tell the oppressed that the empire's cruelty will be answered and that their God is the God of storm and sea, and a refuge for those who shelter in him. The book gives a Judean community a voice to say that the violence done to Thebes and to them is not forgotten. Knowing the audience changes the reading: the vengeance is not a stranger's idea of God but the hope of those under the yoke. It is also a warning for them, since the God who ends Nineveh is the same who ended Samaria.
views: When Assyria's yoke was heaviest (Manasseh is named in Esarhaddon's list of vassals), the oracle would be a hope against the odds.
Judah in the early years of Josiah (630s-620s BC)
As Assyria weakened and Josiah turned away from it (2 Kings 22-23), the oracle would be a victory song in advance. The commonest modern view of the date.
A few read the vivid detail of chapter 2 as written, or reworked, after the fall in 612 BC, and the book as a victory song of the delivered.
Haldar took the book as a liturgy spoken in worship by a cult prophet, so that the audience was the worshiping congregation.

outline: Heading: an oracle about Nineveh, the vision of Nahum of Elkosh
Hymn: the LORD who avenges, comes in storm and shelters those who trust him
The turn between Nineveh and Judah: a plotter, a broken yoke, the herald on the mountains
The destroyer comes: the attack, the flood, the sack
The lions' den and the LORD's challenge
Woe to the city of bloodshed: the prostitute shamed
Thebes fell too: no wall, river or ally helps
Siege orders, locusts, sleeping shepherds and a wound that has no cure

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads Nahum against the 600s BC: Assyria at and after its height, Judah as its vassal under Manasseh and then Josiah, the sack of Thebes in about 663 BC (3:8-10), and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC to the Babylonians and Medes (Babylonian Chronicle ABC 3; Zephaniah 2:13-15; 2 Kings 23:29). It asks what the book says about its own time and how the fall fits it.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks about the date, the unity of the book, the partial alphabet poem of 1:2-8 (Gunkel, Christensen), the hard Hebrew of 1:9-14 and 2:3-8, the cultic reading (Haldar), the link of 1:15 to Isaiah 52:7, and the violent, gendered imagery of 3:4-7 and 3:13 (Weems, Yee, O'Brien and their critics).

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Reads Nahum as the Jewish tradition has handed it down, in the parts this edition has checked: the Twelve counted as one scroll (Bava Batra 13b-15a), the Hebrew order of the Twelve, the link of 1:15 to the herald of Isaiah 52:7 that the Hebrew words themselves show, and the Nahum Pesher from Qumran. The Targum Jonathan, Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak on Nahum were not checked, and no passage of them is quoted.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Reads Nahum as the church has, in the parts this edition has checked: Calvin's lectures on Nahum (on 1:1, 1:2, 1:7, 1:15 and 2:1), Jerome on the place of Elkosh, the herald of 1:15 in Romans 10:15 (which adapts Isaiah 52:7), the prostitute of 3:4 as an image shared with Revelation 17-18, and the puzzle of a book of vengeance after Jonah's mercy. Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Theodore of Mopsuestia and Luther were not checked, and none is quoted.

sections.b:
Nahum is poetry meant to be heard. Its lines are short and full of sound (the whip and wheels of 3:2-3, the "empty, emptied, wasted away" of 2:10, the locusts of 3:15-17). It is best read aloud, in order, with the shifts of speaker noticed: the prophet speaks about the LORD in the hymn, the LORD speaks in 1:12-14, 2:13 and 3:5-7, and the "you" changes between Judah and Nineveh. The notes name the changes.

The book has three moods. The hymn (1:2-8) sets out who God is. The victory song (chapter 2) shows the city falling. The funeral song (chapter 3) names the city's guilt and mourns it as dead. Many readers feel the tension between them, and the Plain keeps it.

sections.h: Why this book has no lens for "still to come"
sections.b: The other prophets in this series have a fifth lens, "still to come" (F). Nahum does not, on purpose. The book looks at the fall of a city that, in its own time, was either about to fall or had fallen. The churches' use of it is as a type: Nineveh as the city of the world, the herald of 1:15 as the preacher of the gospel (Romans 10:15), the prostitute of 3:4 as one of the images Revelation 17-18 shares. Those uses are given in the notes and chapter pages as reception, under the Christian lens, and not as predictions the book makes about a later age.

sections.h: Dating the book: between Thebes and Nineveh
sections.b: Two events fix the limits. Thebes (No-amon) is named in 3:8-10 as a city that has already fallen. Ashurbanipal sacked it about 663 BC, so the book is later than that. Nineveh fell in 612 BC (Babylonian Chronicle), and the book speaks of the fall as coming, not done, or as so near that it can be described. That leaves about 50 years. Within it the commonest view puts the book in the 650s to 620s, when Judah was a vassal and Assyria was beginning to weaken. Josephus (Antiquities 9.11.3), who puts Nahum under Jotham about 115 years before the fall, is not followed. The Plain does not choose a date.

Both books quote the old creed of Exodus 34:6-7 about Nineveh, but with different parts. Jonah 4:2 (and Joel 2:13) take the first half: gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, great in loyal love, one who changes his mind about the harm. Nahum 1:3 takes "slow to anger" and the second half: he will by no means leave guilt unpunished. Both end with a question (Jonah 4:11; Nahum 3:19) and use the same Hebrew word for Nineveh's wickedness (ra'ah, Jonah 1:2; Nahum 3:19). The Twelve places Jonah before Nahum in both its Hebrew and Greek orders, so the reader meets the mercy first. Tobit 14, a deuterocanonical book, speaks of the fall of Nineveh as foretold by a prophet whom the Greek manuscripts name differently: Nahum in Codex Sinaiticus, which the site's Tobit follows, and Jonah in Codex Vaticanus (see the note at 3:7).

Two things in Nahum trouble many readers and are stated plainly here. The first is the picture of the LORD acting as an avenger and of a city destroyed with its children (3:10). The Bible does not hide such things; it holds them next to the rule that vengeance is God's (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19) and to the book of Jonah. The second is the picture of Nineveh as a woman stripped, shamed and displayed (3:5-7), and of the people of the city as "women" (3:13). Critics ask whether this teaches that violence against women is just; others say it is the ancient figure for a conquered city. The Plain translates the Hebrew as written, and the notes at 3:5 and 3:13 give both views.

English verse numbers differ from the Hebrew: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, so English 2:1-13 is Hebrew 2:2-14. The Greek differs again: in Swete's text Greek chapter 1 runs on to "pass through you," and only the last words of English 1:15 ("It is finished, it is taken away") begin Greek chapter 2, so Greek 2:2 is English 2:1 and Greek 2:14 is English 2:13. The notes give the Greek number when quoting it.

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). The Murabba'at scroll Mur88 and the Qumran scroll 4Q82 (4QXII-g), read from the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription, agree with it wherever their letters can be read (they are damaged at several hard places, 1:14 and 2:8, and the variants say which words are restored and so cannot be cited). Where the Greek differs (1:2 to 1:5, 1:7 to 1:12, 1:14, 1:15, 2:1 to 2:3, 2:5 to 2:9, 2:13, 3:1, 3:3, 3:4, 3:8, 3:9, 3:11, 3:13, 3:18) the variants say so. Only Mur88 and 4Q82 are in the site's scroll printout; no other Twelve scroll is claimed to agree. The Plain follows the Masoretic Text at each of these places. It makes no change in the text to fit the alphabet pattern of 1:2-8.

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a commentary on Nahum, 4QpNah (4Q169), copied in the first century BC. It is the only pesher that names historical people: "Demetrius king of Greece," "Antiochus," and the "Lion of Wrath" (usually taken as the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus, who hanged men alive). It reads the "seekers of smooth things" (usually taken as the Pharisees) into Nahum 2 and 3. The Qumran community understood Nahum as speaking of its own day. This is a reception of the book. It does not decide what Nahum meant, and the Plain does not use it as a source for the text. The site's printout carries no text of the pesher, so what is said of it here is from its published editions (Allegro, DJD V; Horgan).

spec.title: Claude's theory: the flood and the wickedness are one verb
spec.body: The Hebrew 'avar, "pass over," appears at the book's beginning of judgment (the flood "passes over" in 1:8), at the turn (the plotter "passes on" in 1:12 and will not "pass through" Judah again in 1:15), and in the last line (Nineveh's wickedness has "passed over" everyone, 3:19). If the repetition is deliberate, the book reads as measure for measure: the flood that passes over Nineveh answers the wickedness that passed over the nations. Two other word-threads (ma'oz, "stronghold," in 1:7 and 3:11; nacham, "comfort," in the prophet's name and 3:7) work the same way. I offer this as my own observation. It overlaps with literary readings of Nahum (O'Brien; Sweeney) but is not taken from them, and the repetition of a common verb proves nothing by itself.

prompts: The storm God and the dry sea

A hand-drawn scroll illustration in ink and soft color of a great storm: a whirlwind with cloud like dust from a giant's feet, a sea going dry with its fish in the mud, and on the dry riverbed a small human figure kneeling under a hilltop fort. Edges soft and torn like old parchment, with cave-drawing figures and a few Hebrew letters in the margins.

A sketch on aged papyrus mixing early Christian art and modern line art: a lone runner with bare feet leaping across mountain ridges at dawn, a scroll in his hand, small figures of festival-goers waking in a village below. Soft uneven borders, no hard rectangle.

A hand-drawn picture in the style of Assyrian palace reliefs softened into brush and ink: a royal lion with a cub and a lioness in a den full of bones, and a ruined palace with open river gates behind them. Edges ragged like old parchment, with a few cuneiform-like marks.
reading: J. J. M. Roberts, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah (Old Testament Library, 1991)
A careful commentary on the Hebrew, with the history of Assyria's fall and the textual problems.
Klaas Spronk, Nahum (Historical Commentary on the Old Testament, 1997)
Detailed on the Hebrew text, the ancient versions and the Near Eastern background.
A reading that takes the violence and gender of the imagery seriously.
A. K. Grayson, Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles (1975)
The Babylonian Chronicle of the fall of Nineveh (ABC 3) in translation.
Marvin A. Sweeney, The Twelve Prophets (Berit Olam, 2000)
Nahum read in its place in the Book of the Twelve.
